extracted.intended_audience: psychologists, journal editors, and researchers studying peer review and scientific publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of journal peer-review practices in psychology, focusing on reviewer reliability, detection of previously published work, sources of bias (especially institutional prestige), and criteria reviewers use to accept or reject manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer reliability / interrater agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of agreement among referees in evaluating a manuscript (interrater agreement). The literature reports low-to-moderate agreement, with intraclass correlation coefficients around 0.55 at best and many studies showing much lower agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by rating scales and statistics (intraclass correlation, Kappa). Examples: Scott (1974) reported 0.26; Ingelfinger (1974) figures below 0.30; Watkins (1979) found near total lack of interrater agreement using Kappa. Low agreement undermines confidence in peer review and suggests chance/reviewer idiosyncrasies may strongly affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of previously published research
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers' and editors' ability to detect that a submitted manuscript has been previously published. In this study, only three of 38 editors/reviewers (8%) detected resubmissions; 92% failed to recognize the manuscripts as previously published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detection rates can be computed including editors/associate editors and reviewers or reviewers only; failure to detect was widespread even for articles from high-impact journals. Implication: reviewers often do not notice prior publication even when identity/affiliation are disguised minimally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological design rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the study's design quality and presence/absence of basic methodological flaws. Reviewers frequently cited 'serious methodological flaws' as grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical methodological criticisms include confounding, lack of randomization, inadequate control of range-of-difficulty across groups, inadequate description of procedures, subject mortality, and design defects that compromise interpretation. These are perennial concerns (not new methodological fads) and are cited as sufficient grounds for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of statistical analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether statistical methods and analyses are correctly chosen and applied (e.g., correct use of ANOVA, avoiding misleading separate analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific reviewer comments include: 'Separate analyses of each test... can be misleading... especially when analyses can be made directly' and 'use of ANOVA for post-tests'. Reviewers check for misuse of statistics (dependent data, assumption violations) and inferential errors; these can prompt rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of presentation and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of writing, organization, and clarity in presenting methods, results, and interpretation. Reviewers criticized manuscripts for being 'confusing', poorly organized, or failing to communicate results clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of critical comments: 'It is all very confusing... the entire presentation of the results needs to be planned more carefully and reorganized' and 'the style of writing leaves much to be desired in terms of communicating to the reader.' Poor clarity can lead to rejection even when underlying data exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty, significance, and contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the manuscript offers new, significant contributions to the field or merely repeats known findings ('adds nothing new').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although in this study rejections were mainly for methodological flaws rather than lack of novelty, reviewers commonly use novelty and contribution as evaluative criteria; explicit statements like 'This point is uninteresting and old' would indicate rejection on these grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias related to author/institutional prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic response bias in favor of authors or institutions with high prestige; major-university referees evaluate major-university authors more favorably than authors from less prestigious institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical support cited (e.g., M. D. Gordon 1980): major-university referees showed favoritism. Mechanisms may include expectancy effects (Rosenthal) or criterion shift (reviewers apply different cutoffs). This bias can advantage well-known institutions and affect fairness of peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of nonblind (open) review on evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of visible author identity and affiliation (nonblind reviewing) on reviewer agreement and potential bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors hypothesize that nonblind journals may show higher reviewer consensus and that knowledge of author/institutional identity could lower or raise the acceptability cutoff (response bias). Limited data are consistent with greater agreement in nonblind settings, but more research is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor role and concurrence with reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors' actions (examining manuscripts and concurring with reviewers) and the impact of editorial policies on decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the sample, every included editor/associate editor indicated examining the manuscript and concurring with reviewers. Changes in editorial policy or scope (e.g., Journal M) can preclude publication regardless of manuscript quality, so editors' judgments and policy shifts are an important evaluation dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer competence and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Competence (expertise and thoroughness) of reviewers selected by editors and its effect on the quality of review outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variation in reviewer competence could explain discrepant decisions across review periods, though large systematic changes by chance are unlikely. Competence is distinct from bias and reliability and is difficult to measure directly but is implicated when reviewers fail to detect obvious issues or prior publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit to journal scope / appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a manuscript is appropriate in topic and format for the target journal; manuscripts outside scope can be rejected outright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One resubmission (to Journal M) was excluded because the journal had changed publication criteria and considered the manuscript inappropriate. Editors sometimes reject on the basis of topical fit rather than methodological quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response bias / criterion shift in decision thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may adopt different decision cutoffs (lowered or raised) for publication acceptability depending on status variables or expectations, producing systematic bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described in signal-detection terms: prestige could validly predict quality or could produce a self-fulfilling effect if reviewers are less rigorous for high-status authors. This affects the ratio of 'hits to misses' and should be considered when interpreting reviewer behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics and procedures for evaluating the peer-review system
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical and procedural tools used to study and quantify peer-review outcomes, including rating scales, intraclass correlation, Kappa, chi-square tests, and resubmission experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the study: use of a 5-point McCartney rating scale to classify reviews, intraclass correlation and Kappa to measure agreement, chi-square to test differences between original and resubmission reviews, and controlled resubmission of previously published articles as an ecological validity method. Researchers should use appropriate statistics and account for regression effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal stability of journal rejection rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a journal's rejection rate and publication criteria remain stable over time, which can affect probability of acceptance on resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors compared historical rejection rates (Table 3) and found overall high and fairly constant rejection rates (~80%) across periods for the journals studied; major shifts in rejection rate or policy could plausibly explain changes in outcomes and should be checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical considerations in evaluating peer review (deception and confidentiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical constraints and procedures when studying peer review directly (e.g., resubmitting published work under fictitious names), including debriefing and requests for confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study substituted fictitious names/institutions and asked participants to keep the study confidential until completion; editors/reviewers were informed when they detected the deception or after study completion. Researchers must weigh the ethics of deception, obtain debriefing, and manage editorial cooperation and potential resistance.
